title: Extension Methods
description: Learn how to add methods to existing types without modifying them.

data.text: **Extension methods** allow you to add new methods to existing types without modifying the original type or creating a new derived type. They are static methods defined in static classes, but they appear as instance methods on the extended type.

Sometimes you want to add behavior to a type you don't control — like `string`, `int`, or `List<T>`. Extension methods let you do this without inheritance, composition, or modifying the original source code. LINQ is a famous example: every LINQ method is an extension method on `IEnumerable<T>`.

terms.definition: A static method defined in a static class, with `this` on the first parameter, that extends an existing type.
The first parameter prefixed with `this` tells the compiler which type is being extended.
Language Integrated Query — a set of extension methods on IEnumerable<T> and IQueryable<T> for querying data.
A class that cannot be instantiated and can only contain static members.

data.text: To create an extension method, follow these rules: define a static class, define a static method, and use the `this` keyword on the first parameter. Once imported with `using`, the method becomes available on instances of the extended type.

data.title: Must Be in a Static Class
data.text: Extension methods must live inside a non-generic static class. They cannot be defined in a non-static class or a generic static class.
You can also extend generic types like `List<T>`, `IEnumerable<T>`, or even your own generic classes. The extended type can be a generic parameter as long as it is the first parameter.

data.title: Generic Extension

data.text: LINQ is the most prominent use of extension methods. Methods like `Where`, `Select`, `OrderBy`, and `GroupBy` are all extension methods on `IEnumerable<T>`. This is why you can call them on arrays, lists, and any collection that implements `IEnumerable<T>`.

data.title: Rules for Extension Methods
items: Defined in a static, non-generic class
The method itself must be static
The first parameter uses the `this` keyword
The extended type cannot be a pointer type
Extension methods cannot access private members of the extended type
Instance methods on the actual type always take precedence over extension methods with the same signature
You must import the namespace containing the static class with `using`

data.title: Use Judiciously
data.text: Extension methods should feel natural and discoverable. Avoid adding methods with ambiguous names, or polluting types like `object` or `string` with unrelated behaviors.

items.question: Do extension methods replace inheritance?
items.answer: No. Extension methods add behavior without access to private state or virtual dispatch. Use inheritance when you need to override or access protected members.

items.question: Why does LINQ use extension methods?
items.answer: LINQ needs to work on any IEnumerable<T> without modifying each collection type. Extension methods let LINQ query methods appear on every enumerable type transparently.

items.question: Can extension methods be overridden?
items.answer: No. Extension methods are static and cannot be overridden. If a real instance method exists with the same signature, the instance method always wins.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Extension methods are static methods with 'this' on the first parameter
They make static methods appear as instance methods
Must be defined in a static, non-generic class
Cannot access private members of the extended type
LINQ is built entirely on extension methods
Use them to add clean, discoverable utility methods to existing types
data.takeaway: Extension methods let you extend types you don't control, making APIs feel natural and fluent.
